title: Ratio of radial to tangential growth about a node yields lanceolate, ovate, cordate leaves

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Ratio of radial to tangential growth about a node yields lanceolate, ovate, cordate leaves

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Dicotyledon leaf shapes arise from growth radial to and transverse to radii about a node of no growth at the leaf base; increasing the ratio of tangential to radial growth carries the outline successively from lanceolate to ovate to cordate.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: If we now alter the ratio between the radial and tangential velocities of growth—in other words, if we increase the angles between corresponding radii—we pass successively through the various configurations which the botanist describes as the lanceolate, the ovate, and finally the cordate leaf.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XVII, “On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms”; topic “Radial co-ordinates and leaf shape”. Scope: leaves of dicotyledons (contrasted with basally growing monocot leaves)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch17-07: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.50

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The predicted sequence is clear, but the proposed mechanism requires developmental velocity fields rather than mature outlines. Existing data can test shape associations and a few species, not the broad dicot mechanism.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: From time-lapse leaf development, estimate radial and tangential growth fields relative to the basal node and test whether their ratio predicts the ordered lanceolate-ovate-cordate transition.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Static herbarium outlines cannot identify growth fields.

Public time-lapse data spanning the three shape classes are sparse.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Mature leaf silhouettes are abundant and can show whether one geometric parameter orders the named shapes. The claim is about velocities of radial and tangential growth, and those velocities are rarely deposited. Outline fits are a proxy that several growth rules can satisfy.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure radial and tangential growth velocities on developing dicot leaves, or, as a weaker proxy, test whether a single ratio of those velocities carries mature outlines from lanceolate through ovate to cordate. Support would be that ordered continuum in the growth data; outlines that require a changing ratio or a different growth centre would refute the mechanism.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Time-lapse and clonal-analysis datasets exist for a few model species and are not a dicot-wide archive.

Pressed outlines do not record growth velocities, which are the variables the mechanism names.
